name: Derived Units
description: Units made by combining the 7 base units together

content.overview: Remember those 7 base units? Turns out you can mash them together like Lego bricks to build every other unit you'll ever need. That's what a derived unit is — nothing new, just base units combined. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
So you've got 7 base units. Cool, but physics also talks about speed, force, energy, power, pressure — where do those come from? Simple: you multiply and divide the base units you already have. {{viz:diagram-02}}

Watch how it builds:

**Speed** = distance ÷ time = meters ÷ seconds = **m/s**

**Force** = mass × acceleration = kilograms × (meters ÷ seconds²) = **kg·m/s²** — which everyone just calls a **Newton (N)**

**Energy** = force × distance = kg·m²/s² — nicknamed the **Joule (J)**

**Power** = energy ÷ time = kg·m²/s³ — nicknamed the **Watt (W)**

See the pattern? Every single one is just base units stacked together. {{viz:chart-01}}

Scientists gave the popular combos catchy names so nobody has to say 'kilograms times meters per second squared' out loud:
- 1 kg·m/s² is a **Newton (N)** — force
- 1 kg·m²/s² is a **Joule (J)** — energy
- 1 kg·m²/s³ is a **Watt (W)** — power

But peel back the label and it's still just the 7 base units doing all the work. {{viz:anim-01}}

Why bother naming them? Because 'newtons' is way faster to say — and read — than spelling out the whole combination every time.
keyPoints: Derived units are just base units multiplied or divided together
Force works out to kg·m/s², nicknamed the Newton
Energy works out to kg·m²/s², nicknamed the Joule
Power works out to kg·m²/s³, nicknamed the Watt
Every derived unit traces back to the 7 base units
content.whyItMatters: Most units you'll bump into in physics are actually derived ones. Once you see how they're built, they stop being random names and start making sense — you can figure out what a unit means just by looking at it.
